subject: electrical-computer
audience: FE Electrical and Computer candidates and engineering students
title: The Feeder That Delivered 228 V Instead of 240 V
featured_title: THE FEEDER THAT DELIVERED 228 V INSTEAD OF 240 V

presentation.challenge: The source measured 240 V. The load saw only 228 V because the feeder resistance was treated as one-way.

practice.primary_question: Why must a single-phase feeder voltage-drop calculation include the full current path?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Using only the one-way conductor resistance when current travels out and back through the circuit.

case_dna.target_misconception: A two-wire single-phase feeder's voltage drop can be found from only one conductor resistance.
case_dna.why_plausible: Cable data often quotes resistance per conductor while the current path uses both outgoing and return conductors.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: With 0.20 Ω per conductor and 30 A, loop resistance is 0.40 Ω, so the drop is 12 V and the load sees 228 V.
case_dna.corrected_model: Use total loop resistance: Rloop = Rout + Rreturn, then ΔV = I Rloop and Ploss = I² Rloop.

problem_statement: A 240 V single-phase source supplies a 30 A load through a two-wire feeder. Each conductor has 0.20 Ω resistance. The design note predicts only a 6 V drop, but the load measures about 228 V. Diagnose the path error, calculate actual voltage drop and feeder loss, and choose a correction that cuts the drop in half.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The source was 240 V. The load received 228 V.
gates.prompt: Which resistance belongs in the voltage-drop path?

options.label: Use both conductor resistances because current flows out and back
options.reason: The series current path includes 0.20 + 0.20 = 0.40 Ω.

options.label: Use only one 0.20 Ω conductor
options.reason: That models only half the path.

options.label: Put the two conductors in parallel
options.reason: They form the outgoing and return path, not parallel branches.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the load voltage
gates.prompt: With 30 A and 0.40 Ω loop resistance, what load voltage (V) do you expect from 240 V?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Measure at the load terminals
gates.result: The load voltage is about 228 V.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the drop
gates.prompt: Use Rloop = 0.20 + 0.20 = 0.40 Ω and ΔV = IR. Enter the voltage drop in V.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The loop model matches the measurement

cards.text: Current flows through both 0.20 Ω conductors.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the feeder note
report: C3. The feeder drop is 30 A × 0.20 Ω = 6 V.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: It uses only one conductor instead of the full loop.

evidence_choices.label: The complete loop is 0.40 Ω, producing 12 V drop

correction.template: Using the full loop, the feeder drop is {drop} V and the load voltage is {load_v} V.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Cut the voltage drop in half
gates.constraint: Keep 240 V source and 30 A load current.

options.label: Reduce each conductor resistance from 0.20 Ω to 0.10 Ω
options.reason: Rloop becomes 0.20 Ω, so drop becomes 6 V.

options.label: Reduce source voltage to 120 V
options.reason: That does not reduce resistive drop at the same current.

options.label: Remove the return conductor from the calculation

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the loop-resistance rule
gates.prompt: A 20 A two-wire feeder has 0.15 Ω per conductor. What is the voltage drop?
gates.explanation: Two-wire feeder drop uses the resistance of both conductors.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the feeder calculation
gates.confirmation: I confirm that single-phase two-wire voltage drop uses the total out-and-back conductor resistance.

items.label: What was assumed
items.value: Only one conductor resistance was included.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use full loop resistance for voltage drop and I²R loss.

seo.seo_title: Feeder Voltage Drop: Why 240 V Becomes 228 V | FE E-030
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Case E-030: a 240 V single-phase feeder delivers 228 V. Use full loop resistance to calculate voltage drop and I²R loss.
seo.excerpt: A feeder calculation can miss half the resistance when it counts only the outgoing conductor and forgets the return path.
seo.direct_answer: For a two-wire single-phase feeder, current travels through both conductors. If each is 0.20 Ω, the loop is 0.40 Ω. At 30 A, the drop is 12 V, so a 240 V source delivers about 228 V.

faqs.q: Do you include both conductors in single-phase voltage drop?
faqs.a: Yes. Use the resistance of the complete out-and-back path.

faqs.q: What is the feeder loss at 30 A and 0.40 Ω?
